newsitem.title: USA: Carey win keeps key labor movement player in game.
newsitem.headline: Carey win keeps key labor movement player in game.

text.p: With Ron Carey's apparent narrow re-election as president of the Teamsters Union, the labor movement keeps a key player in its drive to reinvigorate itself as a social and political force.
At the same time, Carey faces the challenge of healing a deep rift in his own 1.4 million-member union as it seeks to organize workers and prepares for major contract talks.

Carey, 60, declared a divisive year-long battle with the son and namesake of Teamster legend Jimmy Hoffa over Saturday. A court-appointed overseer reported that Carey had captured 52 percent of the eligible votes mailed in by the rank and file during the past month.

The results were not final, since his victory margin of nearly 17,000 votes was smaller than the 41,000 uncounted ballots set aside for eligibility checks. A determining tally may not be completed for a week.

To upset the tentative outcome, however, James Hoffa would need a better than 3-to-1 margin in challenged ballots deemed eligible, a ratio he could not reach even in locals in his Midwestern power base.

Labor scholars said the election results should please leaders of the AFL-CIO, whom Carey helped elect last year with his considerable clout as head of the biggest of the 78 unions in the labor federation.
"There are a lot of people I know in the new leadership of the AFL-CIO who are breathing a sigh of relief," labor historian Michael Kazin of American University said.

Carey shares AFL-CIO President John Sweeney's vision of rebuilding organized labor with massive, vigorous organizing drives aimed particularly at low-wage workers and forging alliances with social activists. The two men also want labor to flex its political muscle, as it tried to do this year with mixed results.
Hoffa, on the other hand, has his father's famous name and image, which AFL-CIO leaders would rather forget, Kazin said.
"When people think of big labor, they think of Jimmy Hoffa," he said. "Sweeney wants them to think of all the young organizers he has out there."

Hoffa, 55, a Detroit labor lawyer, tried during his campaign to conjure up recollections of the glory days of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters under his father. It was considered the strongest union in the country, able to paralyze interstate commerce with a single nationwide strike.
But for some, a different image was formed: of corruption, kickbacks, sweatheart deals, pension fund loans to mobsters and prison terms for three of Carey's six predecessors.

This is the fissure that the election highlighted in a union that represents not only truckers and warehouse workers but flight attendants, miners and a wide array of workers in light industries like food processing, beverages and baking.

"I think you have to realize that there are some pretty deep splits within the union," Michael Belzer of Cornell University's School of Industrial and Labor Relations said. "But the direction is toward grass-roots reform unionism."
Without a leader, Belzer said, backers of Hoffa, who drew 48 percent of the vote, eventually may go along with Carey.
And a united front will be critical if Carey is ever to succeed in converting the decentralized union into an entity that can go up against new and bigger employers, he said.

Unlike the Communications Workers of America, which restructed itself after the breakup of the Bell System, the Teamsters Union has not kept up with the deregulation of the trucking industry, which has spawned many small nonunion firms and multinational giants, Belzer said.
"They are structurally the same union they were 50 years ago," he added.

Challenges Carey will face include trying to organize Federal Express, completing an organizing drive at Union Pacific's Overnite Transportation Co. and signing new contracts next year with United Parcel Service and major long-haul trucking firms that the union struck for three weeks in 1994.
To a large degree, experts said, the name of the union's leader will have little to do with its ability to bargain.
"It just isn't the same as the days before deregulation of the trucking industry," said labor historian Robert Zieger of the University of Florida in Gainsville.

"They're still fighting the basic weaknesses and the competitive pressures that are out there," said Raymond Hilgert, a professor of management and industrial relations at Washington University in St. Louis. "No matter who's at the top, that's not going to change."
